lesson.title: LLM Recap for Agent Builders: Tokens, Context Windows and Sampling
objectives: Explain how a large language model generates text one token at a time.
Describe tokens, the context window and why both limit what an agent can do.
Explain temperature and greedy decoding and choose sensible settings for agents.
Explain why an LLM is stateless and what that means for building agents.
Compute a temperature-scaled softmax over next-token scores.
lesson.definition: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network, usually a transformer, trained to predict the next token in a sequence. At inference time it repeatedly turns the text so far into a probability distribution over its vocabulary, picks a token, appends it and repeats. Every agent in this course uses an LLM as its reasoning engine, so its limits (context size, cost per token, randomness and lack of memory) shape every design decision.

theory.heading: Tokens and next-token prediction
theory.body: Models do not read characters or whole words; they read tokens, which are sub-word pieces produced by a tokenizer. In English one token is roughly four characters, while Hindi or code can use more tokens per word. Generation is autoregressive: the model scores every token in its vocabulary, converts the scores (logits) into probabilities with softmax, chooses one token and feeds the longer sequence back in. This is why output is produced left to right and why long answers take longer and cost more.
points: Pricing, rate limits and context sizes are all measured in tokens.
Input tokens (the prompt) and output tokens (the answer) are usually priced differently; output is more expensive.
Latency grows with the number of output tokens because they are generated one after another.

theory.heading: The context window
theory.body: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one call, counting the system prompt, conversation history, tool definitions, tool results and the answer being generated. An agent fills its context quickly because every tool call and observation is appended to the history. When the limit is reached, something must be dropped or summarised, and models also attend less reliably to facts buried in the middle of very long contexts.
points: Budget = system prompt + tool schemas + history + retrieved data + space reserved for output.
Large windows help but cost more per call and do not guarantee the model uses everything well.
Context management (Days 11–13) is a core agent-engineering skill.

theory.heading: Sampling: temperature, greedy decoding and top-p
theory.body: Softmax with temperature T computes p_i = exp(z_i / T) / sum_j exp(z_j / T). A low temperature sharpens the distribution so the most likely token dominates; a high temperature flattens it and increases variety. Temperature 0 is treated as greedy decoding: always pick the highest-scoring token. Top-p (nucleus) sampling keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. Agents that must emit valid tool calls or JSON usually run at low temperature for consistency, while brainstorming steps can use higher values.
points: Low temperature: more deterministic, better for tool calls, extraction and classification.
High temperature: more diverse, useful for ideation or generating several candidate plans.
Even at temperature 0, hosted models are not guaranteed to be bit-for-bit identical across runs.

theory.heading: Statelessness and what an LLM cannot do alone
theory.body: An LLM API call is stateless: the model remembers nothing between calls, so the application must resend the relevant history every time. A bare model also has a training cut-off, cannot browse, run code, query a database or take actions, and can hallucinate confident but wrong facts. Agentic systems exist to close exactly these gaps: they wrap the model in a loop that supplies memory, calls tools, observes results and checks progress.
points: Memory is an application feature, not a model feature.
Tools give access to fresh data and the ability to act.
Verification steps and grounding reduce the impact of hallucinations.

theory.heading: Why this matters in agent interviews
theory.body: Interviewers often start an agent discussion by checking these basics, because poor answers here lead to poor designs: an engineer who forgets that every loop iteration resends the whole history will underestimate cost and latency, and one who runs tool selection at high temperature will see flaky behaviour. Connect each LLM property to an agent design consequence when you answer.
points: Tokens drive cost and latency of every step in an agent loop.
Context limits drive memory and summarisation strategies.
Randomness drives the need for validation, retries and evaluation.

example.title: How one agent step consumes the context window
example.body: A support agent has a 1,200-token system prompt, 800 tokens of tool schemas and a 3,000-token conversation. It calls an order-lookup tool that returns 1,500 tokens of JSON. The next model call must include all 6,500 tokens plus room for the answer. If the agent loops five times, it resends a growing history each time, so the total input tokens for the task can be several times the size of any single call. The code estimates this with a rough four-characters-per-token rule.

code.source:
def estimate_tokens(text):
    # Rough rule of thumb for English; use the provider's tokenizer for exact counts.
    return max(1, len(text) // 4)

history = ['system prompt ' * 300, 'tool schemas ' * 250]
total_input = 0
for step in range(1, 6):
    history.append('tool result ' * 120)          # each step adds an observation
    call_tokens = sum(estimate_tokens(m) for m in history)
    total_input += call_tokens
    print(f'step {step}: {call_tokens} input tokens')
print('total input tokens for the task:', total_input)

demonstration.description: Apply temperature-scaled softmax to three candidate next tokens with logits Paris = 2.0, Lyon = 1.0 and Delhi = 0.0. Lower temperature concentrates probability on the top token; higher temperature spreads it out; temperature 0 becomes greedy decoding.

code.source:
import math

def softmax(logits, t):
    scaled = [z / t for z in logits]
    m = max(scaled)
    exps = [math.exp(s - m) for s in scaled]   # subtract max for numerical stability
    total = sum(exps)
    return [e / total for e in exps]

for t in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
    print(t, [round(p, 3) for p in softmax([2.0, 1.0, 0.0], t)])

takeaways: LLMs generate text one token at a time from a probability distribution over the vocabulary.
Tokens determine cost, latency and how much fits in the context window.
The context window holds everything: instructions, tools, history, observations and the answer.
Low temperature suits tool calls and structured output; higher temperature suits ideation.
LLM calls are stateless, so agents must manage memory explicitly.
Agents exist to give models memory, tools, feedback and verification they lack on their own.

interview.question: How does an LLM generate a response?
interview.answer: It tokenizes the input, computes a score for every token in its vocabulary, converts the scores to probabilities with softmax, selects a token (greedily or by sampling), appends it and repeats until a stop token or length limit is reached.
interview.explanation: Use the words autoregressive, logits and softmax. Linking token-by-token generation to latency and cost shows you understand the practical consequences.

interview.question: What is a context window, and why does it matter more for agents than for a single chat reply?
interview.answer: It is the maximum number of tokens a model can process in one call, including the prompt, history, tool definitions, tool results and output. Agents append every action and observation, so their context grows each loop and hits the limit far sooner than a simple chat.
interview.explanation: Strong answers mention reserving space for output and strategies such as trimming, summarising or retrieving only relevant memory.

interview.question: What temperature would you use for an agent that selects tools, and why?
interview.answer: A low value, often 0 to 0.3, so the model consistently chooses the most likely tool and produces valid arguments. Higher temperature adds variety, which is a risk when the output must match a schema.
interview.explanation: Add that low temperature does not guarantee correctness, so outputs still need schema validation and retries.

interview.question: LLM APIs are stateless. How then does a chatbot remember the conversation?
interview.answer: The application stores the history and sends the relevant messages with every request. The model only sees what is in the current call's context.
interview.explanation: This is the foundation of agent memory. Mention that resending history increases token cost, which motivates summarisation and retrieval.

interview.question: Why is a raw LLM not an agent?
interview.answer: A raw LLM maps one input to one output. It cannot observe the world, call tools, remember across calls or decide to keep working until a goal is met. An agent wraps the model in a loop with tools, memory and stopping logic so it can pursue a goal over several steps.
interview.explanation: This bridges to Day 2. Interviewers like the framing that the LLM is the reasoning engine while the surrounding system supplies perception, action and control.

practice.title: Temperature-scaled next-token probabilities
practice.objective: Implement the softmax-with-temperature step every LLM uses to choose the next token, including the greedy special case used for reliable tool calls.
practice.statement: Read a temperature and a list of candidate tokens with their logits. Convert the logits to probabilities with softmax(z / T) and print each token with its probability, most likely first. When the temperature is 0, use greedy decoding: the highest-logit token gets probability 1 and every other token gets 0 (if several tokens share the highest logit, the first one in the input wins). Tokens with equal probability keep their input order.
practice.input_format: First line: temperature T (a non-negative number). Each following line: a token and its logit separated by a space.
practice.output_format: One line per token: '<token> <probability>' with the probability to 3 decimal places, sorted by probability descending, ties in input order.
constraints: 1 to 50 tokens; tokens contain no spaces.
Logits are between -50 and 50.
0 <= T <= 10. Subtract the maximum scaled logit before exponentiating for numerical stability.

practice.solution:
import math
import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().splitlines()
t = float(lines[0])
pairs = [line.split() for line in lines[1:] if line.strip()]
tokens = [p[0] for p in pairs]
logits = [float(p[1]) for p in pairs]

if t == 0:
    best = logits.index(max(logits))
    probs = [1.0 if i == best else 0.0 for i in range(len(tokens))]
else:
    scaled = [z / t for z in logits]
    m = max(scaled)
    exps = [math.exp(s - m) for s in scaled]
    total = sum(exps)
    probs = [e / total for e in exps]

order = sorted(range(len(tokens)), key=lambda i: (-probs[i], i))
for i in order:
    print(f'{tokens[i]} {probs[i]:.3f}')
explanation: Parse the temperature and the token/logit pairs.
For T = 0, give probability 1 to the first token with the maximum logit (greedy decoding).
Otherwise divide each logit by T, subtract the maximum to avoid overflow, exponentiate and normalise.
Sort by probability descending, using the input index as a tie-breaker, and print with three decimals.

quiz.question: Which items count against an LLM's context window during an agent step?
options: The system prompt, tool definitions, history, tool results and the generated output
quiz.explanation: Everything the model reads in the call and everything it writes shares the same token limit.

quiz.question: What happens to a softmax distribution as temperature is lowered towards 0?
options: It becomes sharper and the top token dominates
It becomes uniform across all tokens
It has no effect on probabilities
quiz.explanation: Dividing logits by a small T magnifies differences between them, so the highest-scoring token takes almost all the probability.

quiz.question: A chatbot forgets what the user said two turns ago after a code change. What is the most likely cause?
options: The application stopped sending earlier messages with each request
The temperature was set too low
quiz.explanation: LLM calls are stateless; the model only knows the history the application includes in each call.

quiz.question: Logits are A = 1.0 and B = 1.0 at temperature 1. What probability does softmax give token A?
quiz.explanation: Equal logits produce equal exponentials, so each of the two tokens gets half the probability.

quiz.question: An agent frequently emits malformed tool-call arguments. Which change should you try first?
options: Lower the temperature and validate arguments against the tool schema
Switch to a model with a smaller context window
Remove the tool descriptions to save tokens
quiz.explanation: Lower temperature reduces random deviations, and schema validation catches the errors that remain so they can be retried.

lesson.title: What Makes a System Agentic: Autonomy, Goals and the Agency Spectrum
objectives: Define an AI agent and distinguish it from a chatbot, a workflow and a plain program.
Describe the core properties of agentic systems: goal, autonomy, tools, memory and feedback.
Place a system on the agency spectrum based on who controls the flow.
Explain when an agent is the wrong choice and a fixed workflow is better.
Classify example systems by their level of autonomy in code.
lesson.definition: An agentic system is software in which a language model decides, at run time, what to do next in order to reach a goal: which tool to call, which path to take and when the task is finished. The more of the control flow the model owns, the more agentic the system is. A workflow follows steps written by a developer; an agent chooses its own steps inside the boundaries the developer sets.

theory.heading: The core idea: who controls the flow?
theory.body: The most useful test for 'is this an agent?' is to ask who decides the next step. In ordinary software the developer decides with if-statements and loops. In an agent, the model's output decides: it reads the situation, picks an action, observes the result and chooses again. This is why agents can handle open-ended tasks that cannot be scripted in advance, and also why they are harder to predict, test and secure.
points: Goal-directed: works towards an objective rather than answering one message.
Autonomous: chooses actions without a human approving each step.
Tool-using: acts on the world through APIs, code or other systems.
Adaptive: uses feedback from observations to change its next action.

theory.heading: The agency spectrum
theory.body: Agency is a spectrum, not a yes/no label. At level 0 code does everything. At level 1 the model generates text but code decides what happens with it. At level 2 the model makes a single decision such as routing a ticket or choosing one tool call. At level 3 the model runs in a loop, deciding the next action repeatedly and deciding when to stop. Multi-agent systems sit beyond that, with several models coordinating. Naming the level in an interview shows you can match architecture to the problem.
points: Level 0: fixed code, no model in control.
Level 1: single LLM call whose output is used by fixed code.
Level 2: LLM router or one-shot tool call; the model picks one branch.
Level 3: agent loop; the model picks actions until it decides the goal is met.

theory.heading: Workflows versus agents
theory.body: A workflow chains LLM calls and tools along a path written by the developer, for example 'extract fields, then validate, then summarise'. It is predictable, cheaper and easier to test. An agent is better when the number and order of steps depends on what it discovers, as in debugging code or researching a question. Many production 'agents' are mostly workflows with one or two agentic decisions, and that is usually the right choice.
points: Prefer a workflow when steps are known in advance.
Prefer an agent when the path depends on intermediate results.
Start simple and add autonomy only when it measurably improves outcomes.

theory.heading: Building blocks of an agent
theory.body: Most agents are built from the same parts: a model that reasons, instructions that define role and boundaries, tools that let it act, memory that carries information across steps, a control loop that runs until a stopping condition, and guardrails that limit what it may do. Each later day of this course zooms in on one of these blocks.
points: Model (reasoning engine) and instructions (system prompt).
Tools and their schemas.
Memory: short-term context and long-term stores.
Control loop with stopping conditions and step limits.
Guardrails, permissions and human approval points.

theory.heading: Advantages and limitations
theory.body: Agents can complete multi-step tasks, recover from failed attempts and adapt to new inputs without new code. The cost is non-determinism, higher latency and token spend from multiple calls, compounding errors (a 95% reliable step repeated ten times succeeds only about 60% of the time end to end) and a larger security surface because the model can trigger real actions.
points: Strengths: flexibility, multi-step reasoning, self-correction.
Risks: unpredictable paths, error compounding, cost, latency, misuse of tools.
Mitigations: step limits, validation, permissions, human approval and evaluation.

example.title: Three ways to handle a refund request
example.body: Level 1: an LLM drafts a reply and a human sends it. Level 2: an LLM classifies the email as refund, complaint or query, and fixed code routes it. Level 3: an agent reads the email, looks up the order, checks the refund policy tool, asks the customer for a missing invoice number if needed, issues the refund within a limit and writes the reply. The third system handles more cases without new code, but it needs permission limits and logging because it can move money.

takeaways: A system is agentic to the degree that the model decides the next step.
Agency is a spectrum: fixed code, single LLM call, router, autonomous loop, multi-agent.

interview.question: What is an AI agent?
interview.answer: A system in which an LLM pursues a goal by repeatedly deciding which action to take, executing it through tools, observing the result and deciding again until it judges the goal complete or hits a limit.
interview.explanation: Mention goal, autonomy, tools and the feedback loop. Avoid defining an agent as 'a chatbot with a persona'.

interview.question: What is the difference between an agentic workflow and an autonomous agent?
interview.answer: In a workflow the developer fixes the sequence of steps and the model fills in each step. In an autonomous agent the model chooses the sequence itself at run time, including how many steps to take.
interview.explanation: Strong answers say workflows are often the better production choice and give an example of each.

interview.question: When would you not use an agent?
interview.answer: When the steps are known and stable, when strict latency or cost limits apply, when actions are high-risk and must be fully predictable, or when a single well-prompted call already meets the quality bar.
interview.explanation: Interviewers value judgement. Saying 'start with the simplest solution and add autonomy only when evaluation shows it helps' is a strong signal.

interview.question: Why do errors compound in agents, and what do you do about it?
interview.answer: Each step has some failure probability and later steps depend on earlier ones, so end-to-end success is roughly the product of step reliabilities. Mitigations are fewer and simpler steps, validating outputs at each step, retries, checkpoints, step limits and human review for risky actions.
interview.explanation: A quick calculation (0.95 to the power 10 is about 0.6) makes the point memorable.

interview.question: Describe the levels of autonomy you might give an LLM in a product.
interview.answer: Level 0 fixed code; level 1 the model only generates content; level 2 the model makes a single routing or tool decision; level 3 the model runs an action loop and decides when to stop; beyond that, several agents coordinate. Each level adds flexibility and risk.
interview.explanation: Tying levels to controls (approval, permissions, tracing) shows production thinking.

lesson.title: The Agent Loop: Perceive, Reason, Act
objectives: Describe the perceive–reason–act cycle and map it to LLM agent code.
Explain the role of observations, state and feedback in each iteration.
Design stopping conditions: goal reached, step limit, budget and error exits.
Explain why agents can loop forever and how to prevent it.
Implement a bounded control loop that reacts to a changing environment.
lesson.definition: The agent loop is the repeating cycle at the heart of every agent: perceive the current state of the environment, reason about what to do next given the goal, act by calling a tool or producing output, then observe the result and repeat. The loop ends when the goal is met or a safety condition such as a step limit, budget or error stops it.

theory.heading: The three phases
theory.body: Perception gathers the information the agent needs: the user request, the latest tool result, memory and any environment signals. Reasoning is the LLM call, which turns that context into a decision, usually a tool call or a final answer. Action executes the decision in the real world through code, and its result becomes the next perception. The loop exists because one decision rarely completes a non-trivial goal; the agent must see the consequences of its actions to choose the next one.
points: Perceive: build the context from goal, history, observations and memory.
Reason: the model selects the next action or decides to finish.
Act: the runtime executes the action and captures the result.
Observe: the result is appended to state and feeds the next iteration.

theory.heading: From the classic AI agent to the LLM agent
theory.body: Classic AI textbooks describe an agent as anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators, from a thermostat to a robot. LLM agents keep the same structure, but the 'sensors' are tool outputs and messages, the 'actuators' are API calls, and the policy that maps perceptions to actions is a language model guided by a prompt instead of hand-written rules or a trained controller.
points: Reflex agents react to the current percept only.
Goal-based agents choose actions that move towards a goal.
LLM agents are goal-based agents whose policy is expressed in natural language.

theory.heading: State and feedback
theory.body: Each iteration must carry state forward: what has been tried, what was observed and what remains. In simple agents state is just the message history. Without feedback the agent cannot correct mistakes; with it, an agent that sees a failing test or an empty search result can change approach. This closed loop is what lets agents handle environments that change while they work, such as a queue that refills or a file another process edits.
points: Include tool errors in the observation so the model can react to them.
Keep observations concise; huge raw outputs crowd out the goal.
Record each step for debugging and evaluation (trajectories).

theory.heading: Stopping conditions
theory.body: An agent needs explicit exits. The happy path is the model declaring the task done, ideally after a check that the goal really is met. Safety exits include a maximum number of steps, a token or money budget, a wall-clock timeout, repeated identical actions (a sign of a loop) and unrecoverable errors. When a safety exit fires, the agent should return a clear partial result rather than silently failing.
points: Goal check: verify success rather than trusting the model's claim alone.
Step limit and timeout: bound runaway loops.
Budget limit: cap tokens or cost per task.
Loop detection: stop if the same action and arguments repeat without new information.

theory.heading: Limitations of the naive loop
theory.body: A plain loop is easy to build but has weaknesses: each iteration resends a growing history, so cost and latency rise; the model can fixate on a wrong approach; and one bad action can corrupt later steps. Later days add structure on top of the loop: ReAct prompting, planning, memory management, state machines and graphs, retries and human approval.
points: Cost grows with iterations and history length.
Wrong early decisions propagate.
Structure (plans, graphs, checks) makes loops more reliable.

interview.question: Explain the agent loop.
interview.answer: The agent repeatedly perceives the current state (goal, history, latest observation), asks the model to reason about the next action, executes that action through a tool, and feeds the result back as a new observation, until the goal is reached or a stop condition fires.

interview.question: How do you stop an agent from looping forever?

interview.question: How does the agent loop relate to classic AI agent definitions?

practice.solution:
import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
start, target, max_change, max_steps = map(int, lines[0].split())
disturbances = list(map(int, lines[1].split())) if len(lines) > 1 else []

value = start
steps = 0
while True:
    seen = value                                   # perceive
    if seen == target:
        print(f'Goal reached after {steps} actions')
        break
    if steps == max_steps:
        print(f'Stopped: step limit {max_steps} reached at {seen}')
        break
    distance = target - seen                       # reason
    move = min(max_change, abs(distance)) * (1 if distance > 0 else -1)
    value = seen + move                            # act
    if steps < len(disturbances):
        value += disturbances[steps]               # environment changes
    steps += 1
    print(f'Step {steps}: saw {seen}, acted {move:+d}, now {value}')
explanation: Read the configuration and the optional disturbance list.
At the start of every iteration perceive the value and check the goal first, then the step limit.
Choose a move bounded by max_change in the direction of the target.
Apply the action and the disturbance, then print the step so the trajectory is visible.
Re-perceiving each time lets the agent recover from disturbances and overshoots.

lesson.title: ReAct: Interleaving Reasoning and Acting
objectives: Explain how the ReAct pattern interleaves thoughts, actions and observations.
Describe why an explicit reasoning trace improves tool selection and error recovery.
Compare ReAct with act-only and reason-only prompting.
Recognise when ReAct's extra tokens are worth the reliability gain.
Parse and summarise a ReAct trajectory in code.
lesson.definition: ReAct (Reason + Act) is a prompting and control pattern in which the model alternates between a short natural-language reasoning trace, called a thought, and an action such as a tool call. After each action the environment returns an observation, which becomes the next input, and the cycle repeats until the model emits a final answer. The thought helps the model plan and track state, while the action grounds the next thought in real feedback so the agent corrects course instead of hallucinating a result.

theory.heading: What ReAct adds to the plain loop
theory.body: Day 3 showed a loop that perceives, reasons and acts, but the reasoning step can be a single opaque decision. ReAct makes that reasoning explicit: before choosing a tool the model writes a thought such as 'I need the population of France before I can halve it'. That sentence is stored in the context and influences every later step. The action and observation then ground the trace in real data, which is exactly the feedback loop the plain agent needs but does not guarantee.
points: Thought: a short plan, hypothesis or note about what to do next.
Action: a tool call or another defined action.
Observation: the result returned by the environment.
The trace accumulates, so the model can see what it already tried.

theory.heading: The thought-action-observation cycle
theory.body: In a ReAct agent each iteration appends three kinds of text to the transcript. The model first writes a Thought that states its current understanding and the next goal. It then emits an Action, usually a tool name with arguments. The runtime executes the action and appends an Observation containing the result. The model reads the whole transcript on the next call, so the thought becomes evidence of intent and the observation becomes evidence of fact. The loop ends when the model writes a Final Answer or a safety limit fires.
points: One cycle produces a thought, one action and one observation.
The transcript is the agent's working memory within the task.
A final answer should be backed by observations, not by the model's memory alone.

theory.heading: Why reasoning traces improve reliability
theory.body: Forcing the model to state its plan before acting reduces two common failures. First, it improves tool selection because the model must justify the choice, which makes it less likely to reach for an irrelevant tool. Second, it improves recovery because after an error the model can read its own earlier thought and adjust the plan rather than repeating the same call. Studies of ReAct on question-answering and decision tasks found fewer hallucinations than reason-only prompting, because claims that lack an observation become visible in the trace.
points: Thoughts expose the model's plan so mistakes are easier to spot.
Observations provide grounding that pure chain-of-thought lacks.
The trace is also valuable for debugging and evaluation.

theory.heading: Variants and limitations
theory.body: ReAct sits between reason-only methods such as chain-of-thought and act-only methods such as plain tool calling. Variants include adding a self-reflection step after a failure, or restricting the agent to a fixed set of tools. The main cost is tokens: every thought is extra input and output on every iteration, so long traces inflate cost and latency and can crowd the context window. Thoughts can also be confidently wrong, so ReAct does not remove the need for validation and stopping conditions.
points: Reason-only: strong reasoning, no grounding in the environment.
Act-only: grounded but prone to acting on a wrong assumption.
ReAct: grounded reasoning at the cost of more tokens per step.
Reflection and planning patterns build on top of ReAct.

theory.heading: ReAct in practice and in interviews
theory.body: Most modern tool-calling frameworks implement a ReAct-like loop, even when they hide the word 'thought': the model may emit a private reasoning field, then a tool call, then read the result. When you describe ReAct in an interview, connect it to the agent loop from Day 3 and note the trade-off between reliability and token cost. A strong answer also mentions that the thought is not magic, it is just text that conditions the next model call, and that structured tool calls have largely replaced free-text actions for safety.
points: ReAct is a pattern, not a specific library or model feature.
Structured tool calling is the production form of the action step.
Mention cost, context growth and validation when discussing trade-offs.

interview.question: What is the ReAct pattern?
interview.answer: ReAct alternates a natural-language reasoning trace with an action and its observation, repeating until the model reaches a final answer. The thought conditions the next decision and the observation grounds it in the environment.
interview.explanation: Name the three parts, thought, action and observation, and connect the pattern to the agent loop from Day 3.

interview.question: Why does writing a thought before acting improve agent reliability?
interview.answer: It forces the model to commit to a plan and justify its tool choice, which reduces irrelevant tool calls, and it leaves a trace the model can read after an error so it can change approach instead of repeating a failing action.
interview.explanation: Mention both better tool selection and better error recovery, and note that the thought is just conditioning text.

interview.question: How does ReAct differ from chain-of-thought prompting?
interview.answer: Chain-of-thought produces reasoning with no interaction with the world. ReAct adds actions and observations, so each reasoning step can be checked against real tool output rather than relying on the model's memory.
interview.explanation: The key difference is grounding. Reason-only methods cannot detect a wrong assumption until the final answer is wrong.

interview.question: What are the main costs of ReAct?
interview.answer: Extra tokens on every iteration for the thoughts and observations, higher latency, faster context growth, and the risk that a confident but wrong thought steers the agent off course.
interview.explanation: Trade-off answers are strong. Add mitigations such as concise thoughts, context trimming and validation of actions.

interview.question: Would you use free-text ReAct actions or structured tool calls in production, and why?
interview.answer: Structured tool calls, because the runtime validates the tool name and arguments against a schema, which prevents malformed actions and injection through free text. The reasoning trace can still be kept as a private thought field.
interview.explanation: This bridges to Day 5 and shows you understand the safety and reliability advantages of schema-bound actions.

lesson.title: Tool and Function Calling: Giving the Model Hands
objectives: Explain how function calling turns model output into structured tool invocations.
Describe a tool schema and the role of names, parameters and descriptions.
Design tools that are easy for a model to select and use correctly.
Validate tool arguments against a schema and return errors the model can fix.
Validate a tool call against its schema in code.
lesson.definition: Tool calling, also called function calling, is a mechanism in which the model is given a list of tools described by schemas and can respond not with prose but with a structured request to invoke one of them. The application executes the tool, returns the result as a message, and the model continues. It is the bridge between reasoning and action: the model decides what to call and with which arguments, while ordinary code performs the call and enforces the rules.

theory.heading: From text to structured calls
theory.body: Early agents asked the model to write an action as free text such as 'search[weather]', and the application parsed it. That is fragile: the model can misspell the tool, forget a bracket or invent a parameter. Function calling replaces the parsing with a contract. The provider exposes the tools as a schema and the model emits a structured object with a tool name and typed arguments, so the runtime can validate before executing anything.
points: The model chooses the tool and supplies arguments; the runtime executes it.
Arguments arrive as a structured object rather than text to parse.
The provider usually guarantees the call matches the declared schema.

theory.heading: Anatomy of a tool schema
theory.body: A tool schema has a name, a description and a parameter list, where each parameter has a type, a description and whether it is required. The name should be a clear verb, the description should say what the tool does and when to use it, and the parameter descriptions should explain the expected values. The model reads these descriptions to decide which tool to call, so vague or overlapping descriptions are a leading cause of wrong tool selection.
points: Name: short and action-oriented, for example get_weather or create_ticket.
Description: what it does, when to use it and what it returns.
Parameters: typed fields marked required or optional, with enums for fixed choices.
Return shape: keep results small and structured so they fit the context.

theory.heading: The execution contract
theory.body: The application owns execution. It receives the call, validates the arguments, checks permissions, runs the tool and returns a result message. Errors must be caught and returned as observations, not raised, so the model can correct bad arguments on the next turn. Results should be concise and in a predictable shape, because large or noisy tool output wastes context and confuses later reasoning.
points: Validate arguments before running the tool.
Enforce authorisation and rate limits at execution time, not in the prompt.
Return errors as structured observations so the model can retry.
Truncate or summarise large results before adding them to the context.

theory.heading: Designing tools the model can use
theory.body: Good tool design follows a few rules. Keep the number of tools small and their purposes distinct, so the model is not forced to guess between similar options. Prefer several focused tools over one tool with a mode flag. Make destructive or expensive actions explicit and gated. Return stable field names, because the model learns to rely on them, and document the exact result format in the description.
points: Few, distinct, well-named tools beat many overlapping ones.
Prefer specific tools over a single 'do anything' tool.
Gate irreversible actions behind confirmation or a permission check.
Document the result shape so the model can use it reliably.

theory.heading: Limitations and failure modes
theory.body: Tool calling is reliable but not infallible. The model can still pick the wrong tool when descriptions overlap, pass a plausible but wrong value, or call a tool it does not need. Providers may not support parallel calls or may reorder them. And because the model can trigger real side effects, tool calling widens the security surface: a malicious tool result or user message can try to steer the model into a harmful call, which is why authorisation belongs in code, not in the prompt.
points: Ambiguous descriptions cause wrong tool selection.
Values can be well-typed but semantically wrong.
Never trust the model for permissions; enforce them in code.
Log every call and result for debugging and audit.

When the user asks about Paris in Celsius, the model does not write prose; it returns a structured call naming the tool and filling the arguments. The runtime validates the arguments, runs the tool and appends the result for the model to summarise.

interview.question: What is function calling?
interview.answer: A mechanism where the model is given tool schemas and can respond with a structured request to call one, including typed arguments. The application validates and executes the call, then returns the result so the model can continue.
interview.explanation: Emphasise the split of responsibilities: the model decides, the code executes and enforces rules.

interview.question: What makes a good tool description?
interview.answer: It states what the tool does, when to use it, what each parameter means and what the result looks like. It is specific enough to distinguish the tool from similar ones, because the model chooses between tools by reading these descriptions.
interview.explanation: Mention that overlapping descriptions are a common cause of wrong tool selection, and that enums reduce invalid values.

interview.question: How should an agent handle a tool that returns an error?
interview.answer: Catch the error and return it as a structured observation with enough detail for the model to fix the arguments or choose another tool, rather than crashing the loop. Do not leak secrets or stack traces.
interview.explanation: This connects to the error-handling point from the agent loop and keeps the agent self-correcting.

interview.question: Why is it dangerous to rely on the prompt for permissions?
interview.answer: A prompt is just text the model may be talked out of following, especially by injected content in a tool result. Authorisation, rate limits and destructive-action gating must be enforced in code at execution time.
interview.explanation: This previews prompt-injection defence and shows you treat the model as untrusted for security decisions.

interview.question: Would you give an agent one general tool or several specific tools?
interview.answer: Several specific tools, because a single tool with a mode flag forces the model to encode intent in a parameter it may get wrong, and it makes validation and permissions coarser. Specific tools have clear names, typed arguments and narrow effects.
interview.explanation: Connect tool granularity to validation, safety and selection accuracy.

lesson.title: Planning and Task Decomposition
objectives: Explain how planning turns a high-level goal into an ordered set of sub-tasks.
Describe plan-and-execute and why plans are often revised mid-task.
Recognise dependencies between sub-tasks and order them correctly.
Compare upfront planning with step-by-step ReAct reasoning.
Produce a valid execution order from a set of task dependencies in code.
lesson.definition: Planning is the agent skill of breaking a goal into smaller sub-tasks and deciding the order in which to do them before or while acting. Task decomposition produces the sub-tasks; a plan records their sequence and dependencies. A good plan makes progress visible, exposes parallelism and gives the agent checkpoints, but it must stay revisable because real environments return surprises that invalidate the original plan.

theory.heading: Why agents need plans
theory.body: ReAct reasons one step at a time, which is flexible but myopic: the agent can wander, repeat work or lose the thread on a long task. A plan gives the agent a map. It decomposes a goal such as 'prepare a competitor report' into sub-tasks such as gather sources, extract pricing, compare features and draft a summary. With a plan the agent can track what is done, what is next and what depends on what, which reduces loops and makes the task easier to evaluate.
points: Decomposition turns an open-ended goal into concrete, checkable sub-tasks.
A plan records order and dependencies between sub-tasks.
Checkpoints make partial progress and failures visible.

theory.heading: Plan-and-execute versus interleaved reasoning
theory.body: In the plan-and-execute pattern the agent first writes a full plan, then executes each step, optionally replanning when a step fails or reveals new information. This contrasts with interleaved ReAct, which decides the next action without committing to a whole plan. Plan-and-execute is cheaper for long, structured tasks because the plan is written once, while ReAct adapts faster to surprises. Many systems combine them: a short plan, executed with ReAct-style steps inside each step.
points: Plan-and-execute: write the plan, then carry it out step by step.
ReAct: decide one action at a time with no fixed plan.
Hybrid: a coarse plan with flexible reasoning inside each step.

theory.heading: Dependencies and ordering
theory.body: Sub-tasks rarely stand alone. Extracting pricing depends on having gathered sources; drafting the report depends on the comparison. These dependencies form a directed graph, and a valid execution order is a topological order in which every task comes after the tasks it depends on. When several tasks are ready at once they can be run in parallel, and when a cycle appears in the graph the plan is impossible and must be rewritten.
points: A dependency means the earlier task's output is needed by the later one.
A topological order respects every dependency.
Independent tasks can run in parallel to save time.
A dependency cycle means the plan cannot be executed as written.

theory.heading: Replanning and failure
theory.body: A plan is a hypothesis, not a guarantee. A step can fail, return unexpected data or make a later step unnecessary. Robust agents detect this and replan: mark the failed step, decide whether to retry, substitute or abandon it, and regenerate the remaining plan. Replanning should be bounded so the agent does not thrash, and each revision should preserve the work already completed rather than starting over.
points: Detect failure or invalidation at each step before continuing.
Replan the remaining work instead of discarding finished work.
Bound the number of replans to avoid an endless plan-rewrite loop.
Keep the original goal fixed while the path to it changes.

theory.heading: Limitations of planning
theory.body: Planning is only as good as the model's understanding of the domain and the tools available. An over-detailed plan can be brittle and wrong, and a plan made before any exploration can miss the real difficulty of a task. Plans also add tokens and latency, and they can create false confidence if the agent follows a bad plan without checking. The practical rule is to plan coarsely, verify each step, and replan often enough to stay aligned with reality.
points: Plans based on assumptions fail when the assumptions are wrong.
Over-detailed plans are brittle; coarse plans are more adaptable.
Always verify step outputs rather than trusting the plan blindly.

interview.question: Why do agents need planning at all?
interview.answer: Step-by-step reasoning can wander or repeat on long tasks. A plan decomposes the goal into concrete sub-tasks with an order and dependencies, which keeps progress visible, enables checkpoints and makes the task easier to evaluate.
interview.explanation: Contrast planning with pure ReAct and mention that plans must stay revisable.

interview.question: Compare plan-and-execute with ReAct.
interview.answer: Plan-and-execute writes the whole plan first and then runs it, which is cheaper for long structured tasks. ReAct decides one action at a time, which adapts faster to surprises but can lose the thread. Many systems combine a coarse plan with ReAct-style reasoning inside each step.
interview.explanation: The trade-off is commitment and efficiency versus adaptivity. Naming the hybrid shows practical experience.

interview.question: How do you handle dependencies between sub-tasks?
interview.answer: Model them as a directed graph and execute in a topological order so each task runs after the tasks it depends on. Independent tasks can run in parallel, and a cycle means the plan is invalid and must be rewritten.
interview.explanation: Mention that a cycle is a design error, not something to retry, and that parallel branches cut wall-clock time.

interview.question: When should an agent replan?
interview.answer: When a step fails, returns unexpected data, or makes a later step unnecessary. The agent marks the affected steps, keeps completed work, and regenerates only the remaining plan, with a bound on how many times it may replan.
interview.explanation: Interviewers look for bounded replanning that preserves progress rather than restarting the whole task.

interview.question: What are the risks of a very detailed upfront plan?
interview.answer: It is brittle: a wrong assumption early on invalidates many later steps, it costs tokens and latency to generate, and the agent may follow it without checking reality. Coarse plans with per-step verification are usually more robust.
interview.explanation: This shows judgement about planning depth and the value of verification over blind plan-following.

lesson.title: Agent Memory: Short-Term Context and Long-Term Stores
objectives: Distinguish short-term working memory from long-term memory in an agent.
Explain why the context window cannot be the only memory an agent uses.
Describe summarisation, retrieval and trimming as context-management strategies.
Choose what to write to a long-term store and when to read it back.
Manage a fixed token budget with a sliding-window policy in code.
lesson.definition: Agent memory is the information an agent can use beyond the current model call. Short-term memory is the working context of the current task: the messages, tool results and notes inside the context window. Long-term memory is anything stored outside the model, such as a vector database, key-value store or file, and read back when relevant. Memory lets an agent act consistently across many steps and many sessions, which a stateless model cannot do on its own.

theory.heading: Two kinds of memory
theory.body: Short-term memory lives inside the context window and lasts for the current task. It holds the system prompt, the conversation so far, the latest observations and any scratchpad notes. Long-term memory lives outside the model and persists across tasks and sessions: past conversations, learned user preferences, documents and facts. The context window is fast but small and expensive; a long-term store is larger and persistent but must be searched, so an agent needs a policy for moving information between them.
points: Short-term: the working context of the current run, lost when the run ends.
Long-term: external storage that survives across runs and sessions.
Semantic memory stores facts; episodic memory stores past events and interactions.
Moving information between the two is an explicit design decision.

theory.heading: Why the context window is not enough
theory.body: Every token in the context costs money and latency and counts against a hard limit, and models attend less reliably to facts buried in the middle of very long contexts. An agent that keeps appending observations will eventually overflow or degrade. It also forgets everything between runs, because the model is stateless. Long-term memory solves persistence, while context management solves the size and cost problem within a run.
points: The window is a fixed budget shared by prompt, history, tools and output.
Long contexts are slower, pricier and less reliable in the middle.
Without external memory the agent restarts from zero every session.

theory.heading: Context-management strategies
theory.body: When the context fills up the agent must compress or drop content. Trimming keeps only the most recent messages, which is simple but can lose important early instructions. Summarisation replaces old turns with a shorter summary, keeping meaning at the cost of detail and an extra model call. Retrieval keeps the context small by fetching only the memories relevant to the current step. Production agents often combine all three: summarise old history, trim low-value messages and retrieve the few most relevant long-term items.
points: Sliding window: keep the newest items that fit the budget.
Summarisation: compress old history into a running summary.
Retrieval: pull only the relevant stored memories into context.
Always reserve space for the model's own output.

theory.heading: Writing to and reading from long-term memory
theory.body: Long-term memory only helps if the agent decides what to store and when to recall it. Writing should capture durable, reusable facts such as user preferences, resolved issues and outcomes, rather than every raw message. Reading usually works by embedding the current situation and searching for similar stored items. Both directions need care: storing everything creates noise, and retrieving too much re-creates the overflow problem the store was meant to solve.
points: Write durable facts and outcomes, not every transient message.
Embed and index memories so they can be searched by meaning.
Retrieve a small, ranked set of items per step.
Let the user inspect and delete stored memories for trust and compliance.

theory.heading: Limitations and risks
theory.body: Memory introduces new failure modes. A stale fact can contradict the present, a wrong memory can be retrieved confidently, and summarisation can drop the one detail that mattered. Writing the wrong thing to a shared store can leak one user's data to another. Good memory design therefore includes timestamps, scoping per user or tenant, validation before writing, and a way to expire or correct memories. In interviews, treat memory as a system with its own data lifecycle, not a single database call.
points: Stale or incorrect memories cause confident errors.
Summaries lose detail and can omit critical facts.
Scope memories per user or tenant to prevent leaks.
Add expiry, correction and audit paths to the memory store.

Write durable facts and outcomes to long-term memory, not every message.

interview.question: What is the difference between short-term and long-term memory in an agent?
interview.answer: Short-term memory is the working context of the current run, such as messages, observations and notes inside the context window. Long-term memory is external storage that persists across runs, such as a vector store or database, and is read back when relevant.
interview.explanation: Add that short-term memory is fast but limited and ephemeral, while long-term memory is larger and persistent but must be searched.

interview.question: Why can't the context window be the agent's only memory?
interview.answer: It is a fixed, expensive budget shared by the prompt, history, tools and output, models attend less reliably to long contexts, and it is cleared between runs because the model is stateless. External memory provides persistence and lets the agent keep the working context small.
interview.explanation: Mention cost, latency, the unreliable middle of long contexts and statelessness.

interview.question: Describe three ways to keep the context from overflowing.
interview.answer: Trim old messages with a sliding window, summarise old history into a running summary, and retrieve only the few long-term memories relevant to the current step. Reserve space for the model's output and combine the strategies.
interview.explanation: Naming all three, and the need to reserve output space, shows practical context engineering.

interview.question: What should an agent write to long-term memory?
interview.answer: Durable, reusable facts and outcomes such as user preferences, resolved issues and important results, rather than every raw message. Writing everything creates noise and retrieval problems.
interview.explanation: Add that memories should be scoped per user or tenant, timestamped, validated and expirable.

interview.question: What new risks does adding a memory store create?

import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().splitlines()
budget = int(lines[0].strip())
n = int(lines[1].strip())
messages = []
for i in range(2, 2 + n):
    tokens, _, text = lines[i].partition(' ')
    messages.append((int(tokens), text))

kept = []
total = 0
for tokens, text in reversed(messages):
    if total + tokens > budget:
        break
    total += tokens
    kept.append((tokens, text))
kept.reverse()

for tokens, text in kept:
    print(f'{tokens} {text}')
print(f'Kept: {len(kept)}, Dropped: {n - len(kept)}')

Walk the messages from newest to oldest, accumulating the token cost.
Keep a message only while the running total stays within budget, and stop at the first that overflows.
